title: The Alpha File
author: Benjamin Riley
summary: Benjamin Riley announces a new landing page for his investigative reporting on Alpha School and publishes his seventh report, on student motivation. The report argues that Alpha School markets itself as building intrinsic motivation through its link to UT-Austin psychologist David Yeager and the Alpha Motivation Lab, while former students, guides and observers describe a culture built entirely on extrinsic rewards and punishments such as the Rocket Ship and Pirate Ship tiers. Riley sets this against the research literature, including a meta-analysis of more than 223,000 students, which finds that avoiding-punishment motivation does not help performance and harms well-being. He then traces Yeager's ties to the school through the lab's trademark filings, its funding from the Future of Education LLC, a co-authored paper with a founder's daughter, and events with MacKenzie Price. Riley says Yeager declined to address the school's motivational practices, and concludes that the school is using his reputation to cloak them.
points: Former guides, a former student and an outside observer all describe Alpha School motivation as points, status tiers, privileges and isolation, with no sign of cultivating intrinsic motivation.
The research Riley cites favours the carrot over the stick when extrinsic methods are used at all, and finds punishment-avoidance motivation linked to diminished well-being.
Yeager's own work stresses safety, belonging and mentoring, which Riley argues is the opposite of a rewards-and-punishments system with segregated tiers.
Trademark filings, funding sources and a co-authored paper connect the Alpha Motivation Lab to the school's owners, which Riley presents as a conflict that needs explaining.
Riley moves his Alpha reporting to a dedicated sub-page and signals that he will next examine the school's leadership and the culture it created.
quotes: Alpha School claims that it incorporates motivational techniques that arise from Yeager’s leading work in this field. In reality, however, Alpha School does not follow Yeager’s methods in the slightest, and instead employs an entirely extrinsic method of rewards and punishments.

Without exception, they have described a school culture and pedagogical approach wherein everything is based on obtaining rewards and status (e.g., the Rocket Ship), or else having certain privileges taken away (e.g., the Pirate Ship), as described in my prior reporting:
Within the education field, there is extensive research and debate regarding the respective roles that intrinsic versus extrinsic motivation should play to motivate student learning.

This recent meta-analysis of more than 223,000 students found that motivation based on avoiding punishment was not associated with academic performance or persistence, but was associated with diminished well-being.

His position, if I’ve understood it correctly, appears to be diametrically at odds with Alpha School’s wholly extrinsic pedagogy, and especially with respect to Alpha’s use of punishments and “othering” of students that struggle academically — e.g., the Pirate Ship.
It’s a snow job, and while I totally get why Alpha School’s leaders are doing it, the question is why David Yeager appears willing to go along with their charade.

Yeager should be explicitly and publicly disavowing what Alpha School is doing to extrinsically motivate children through rewards and (especially) punishments. That he’s chosen silence instead speaks volumes to the corrupting power of money in academia.
